In collider experiments, "hands-on maintenance" typically refers to the ability to work on equipment with minimal or no waiting time for radioactive decay after shutdown. Dense alloys with high Z materials (especially tungsten-based alloys) can have significant induced radioactivity issues, particularly if they contain elements that form long-lived isotopes.

The term "standard structural absorber" for F2 suggests it might be something like steel or aluminum, which are typically safe for hands-on maintenance. The "dense alloys" (F1 and F3) are more likely to be tungsten-based, which can have radioactivation issues.

However, I don't see explicit information about radioactivation or hands-on maintenance compatibility in the documents. Let me check if there's any hidden information I might have missed. Dense alloys with short radiation lengths are typically tungsten-based. Tungsten can produce W-181 and W-188 isotopes that can remain active. "Standard structural absorber" (F2) suggests iron/steel, which typically allows hands-on maintenance.
